title: AI shoved into every app

alt.text: A sprinkle of AI where it helps, against AI shoved into an app that did not need it.

youtube.title: Every App Is Shoving AI at Us. We Did This With Web3
youtube.description:
Sometimes I just need a code editor. Not an agent orchestrator. Not a copilot. A code editor.

I made a video recently about Windsurf becoming an agentic desktop, where the whole point is orchestrating and managing agents. Cursor went the same way. A lot of editors are going the same way. And that’s fine, except it’s now the only direction on offer.

This is why I have been using Zed. The AI integration is there when I want it, and it isn’t in my face when I don’t.

What I actually loved about Cursor was never the agents. It was writing my own code with good autocomplete and tab suggestions. That’s what I was there for. When that stopped being the centre of the product, I stopped using it.

I do understand why it happens. Companies go where the hype is. Nobody wants to look like they’re lagging. But at some point it stops being about what users are asking for and starts being about what impresses investors.

Some AI features genuinely work. A sprinkle here and there, in the right place. The tiring part is the apps that didn’t need it at all getting it anyway.

We’ve done this before. A few years ago it was Web3, and everyone was going to rebuild their app on the blockchain. Clients came to me with app projects and listed Web3 integration as a main feature. I’d look at it, think this is completely unnecessary, then build it anyway, because I was being paid.

And then it settled. Now we do Web3 integrations when they’re genuinely needed, not because everyone is talking about it.

AI isn’t going anywhere, and it’s a real invention. I’m just waiting for the part where it settles and stops being shoved down everyone's throat.

Everything in one place: https://braandly.bio/ayomideodewale

linkedin.body:
Sometimes I just need a code editor. Not an agent orchestrator, not a copilot. An editor.

Windsurf is becoming an agentic desktop, built around orchestrating agents. Cursor went the same way. Most editors are heading there. Each is a reasonable product decision. Collectively it means there’s now one direction on offer.

What I liked about Cursor was never the agents. It was the tab suggestions, and writing the code myself with something good sitting next to me. Once that was no longer what the product was for, I moved off it. I use Zed now, where the AI integration is there when I want it and out of the way when I don’t.

I understand the pressure. Companies go where the hype is, and nobody wants to look like they’re lagging. But there’s a point where the roadmap stops answering what users asked for and starts answering what impresses investors, and users can tell the difference.

We have run this exact cycle before. A few years ago clients came to me with app briefs where Web3 integration was listed as a main feature. Connect to the blockchain, because that’s what everyone was doing. I would look at the product, think this is genuinely unnecessary, and then build it, because I was being paid to build it.

It settled eventually. Now Web3 integration happens when there’s a real reason for it, and the work is better for it.

AI isn’t Web3. It’s far more useful and it isn’t going anywhere. But the adoption pattern is the same one, and the same correction is coming: the sprinkle in the right place survives, the feature bolted on to look current doesn’t.

If you’re putting AI in your product this quarter, the useful test is simple. Would you still ship it if no investor ever saw the roadmap?
